title: HE COULD DEFEND EVERY VERSE… BUT COULDN’T DEFEND THE WAY HE TREATED PEOPLE.
paragraphs: HE COULD DEFEND EVERY VERSE… BUT COULDN’T DEFEND THE WAY HE TREATED PEOPLE.
He was quick to correct everyone's theology—until one uncomfortable question exposed the difference between knowing the Word of God and allowing the Word of God to change him.
He knew the Scriptures.
He knew the Greek.
He knew the Hebrew.
He could explain why your favorite preacher was wrong, why your interpretation was questionable, and why your understanding of grace needed correction.
He could dismantle a theological argument in minutes.
But one evening, someone asked him a question that no seminary lecture, commentary, or theological debate had prepared him to answer.
“If you know Jesus so well… why is it so difficult to see Jesus in the way you treat people?”
Silence.
Not because he couldn't find a verse.
He had hundreds.
Not because he couldn't construct an argument.
He had spent years learning how.
But because, for the first time in a very long time, someone wasn't questioning what he believed.
They were questioning what his beliefs had made of him.
And the most frightening possibility was beginning to settle into his heart.
What if he had become exceptionally skilled at defending the truth while quietly resisting the very truth he defended?
Stay with this.
Because somewhere between the next few paragraphs and the final Scripture, you may discover that this story isn't really about him.
It might be about you.
And if we're willing to be painfully honest, it might be about me too.
He wasn't a villain.
That's what made the story so uncomfortable.
He loved studying the Bible. He genuinely cared about sound doctrine. He believed false teaching could damage souls, and he wasn't wrong.
Scripture itself commands believers to hold firmly to faithful teaching and refute what contradicts it (Titus 1:9).
Truth matters.
Doctrine matters.
What we believe about Jesus matters eternally.
But somewhere along the way, something subtle had happened.
His love for truth had begun to mingle with his love for being right.
At first, nobody noticed.
He simply wanted people to understand Scripture accurately.
Then he started enjoying the feeling of catching mistakes.
A poorly worded sermon became an opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge.
A struggling believer asking an imperfect question became another theological problem to correct.
A new Christian sharing an awkward testimony became someone whose language needed immediate refinement.
And every time he won an argument, something inside him whispered that he had defended God's honor.
Sometimes he had.
But sometimes he had merely defended his own pride using God's name.
That distinction is terrifying.
Because pride doesn't always walk into church wearing expensive clothes and demanding applause.
Sometimes pride carries a Bible.
Sometimes it quotes Scripture accurately.
Sometimes it speaks confidently about holiness while refusing to apologize to the people it has wounded.
And sometimes it mistakes the satisfaction of winning an argument for the fruit of the Holy Spirit.
He could recognize heresy from a distance.
But he couldn't recognize contempt in his own voice.
He could explain biblical reconciliation.
But he hadn't spoken to a family member in months because neither wanted to admit being wrong.
He could teach about the patience of God.
But his children were becoming afraid to ask him questions.
He could preach about the gentleness of Christ.
But his wife had learned to choose her words carefully around him.
And when someone confronted him about the contradiction, he reached for the one weapon that had never failed him.
Another Bible verse.
Only this time, the verse wasn't enough to silence the question.
Because the question was not whether Scripture was true.
The question was whether he was obeying it.
There is a moment in the Gospel of John that should disturb anyone who has ever mistaken biblical knowledge for spiritual maturity.
Jesus speaks to religious leaders who diligently searched the Scriptures.
They were not ignorant men.
They took the sacred writings seriously.
Yet Jesus told them:

“You search the scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.” — John 5:39–40, World English Bible
The Greek phrase in verse 40 is devastating:
καὶ οὐ θέλετε ἐλθεῖν πρός με
Kai ou thelete elthein pros me.
“And you are unwilling to come to me.”
Notice what Jesus exposed.
Their problem was not a lack of access to Scripture.
Their problem was an unwillingness to come to the One to whom Scripture pointed.
They were studying the testimony while resisting its central Person.
They were examining the words while rejecting the living Word standing before them.
And suddenly, the danger becomes personal.
You can know the biblical languages and still need to repent.
You can explain justification and still struggle to extend forgiveness.
You can understand sanctification and still resist the Spirit's correction.
You can accurately describe the humility of Christ while refusing to humble yourself before the people you've hurt.
None of this makes theology unnecessary.
It makes genuine theology more necessary than ever.
Because sound doctrine should lead us toward the living Christ, not merely toward greater confidence in ourselves.
Paul understood this.
He was no enemy of theological precision. His letters contain some of the deepest doctrinal teaching in Scripture.
Yet he also wrote:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” — 1 Corinthians 8:1, WEB
The Greek is remarkably vivid.
ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ, ἡ δὲ ἀγάπη οἰκοδομεῖ
Hē gnōsis physioi, hē de agapē oikodomei.
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
The verb physioi carries the image of being inflated or puffed up.
The verb oikodomei speaks of building up.
One swells the ego.
The other strengthens another person.
Paul's immediate concern was knowledge used without loving consideration for others in the controversy over food offered to idols. He was not condemning biblical knowledge itself.
He was exposing what happens when knowledge becomes detached from love.
And that distinction reaches into our churches, our homes, our comment sections, and our private conversations.
When you correct someone, are you trying to build them up?
Or are you trying to prove that you're above them?
When you respond to a theological mistake, do you care about the person making it?
Or have they become nothing more than an opponent to defeat?
When someone disagrees with you, do you still see a human being made in God's image?
Or do you immediately see a target?
These are not small questions.
Because it is possible to speak true words with a heart that desperately needs correction.
And then comes the Scripture that leaves almost no room for excuses.
“The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him.” — 2 Timothy 2:24–25, WEB
Read that again.
The Lord's servant must be able to teach.
Yes.
But also gentle.
Patient.
Willing to correct without becoming quarrelsome.
Biblical correction is not forbidden.
It is commanded in the appropriate circumstances.
But the manner of correction is not irrelevant to the God whose truth we claim to represent.
The Greek word translated “gentle” in verse 24 is:
ἤπιον — ēpion
It describes gentleness, not weakness.
And verse 25 speaks of correcting opponents with:
πραΰτητι — prautēti
Gentleness or meekness.
This is not permission to compromise the Gospel.
It is a command to refuse the arrogance that can disguise itself as courage.
Jesus Himself confronted hypocrisy, rebuked false teaching, and spoke with extraordinary authority.
But He also welcomed the weary, restored the broken, showed compassion to sinners, and humbled Himself in obedience to the Father.
We cannot take His boldness while rejecting His humility and claim to be imitating Him faithfully.
That evening, the man finally stopped talking.
The person who had challenged him was not trying to humiliate him.
They were exhausted.
Exhausted from being corrected but rarely heard.
Exhausted from watching biblical discussions become contests.
Exhausted from hearing beautiful explanations of Christian love that seemed to disappear whenever someone disagreed.
Then came another question.
Softer this time.
Almost trembling.
“When was the last time you admitted you were wrong without explaining why you were still mostly right?”
He looked away.
He remembered the arguments.
The messages.
The conversations he had replayed in his mind, congratulating himself for the responses he should have given.
He remembered people who had stopped opening up to him.
He had assumed they were unwilling to receive truth.
Perhaps some were.
But had he ever considered that others might have been afraid of how he would respond?
And then another memory surfaced.
His child, standing in the doorway.
Trying to explain a mistake.
He remembered interrupting.
Correcting.
Lecturing.
He remembered how quickly the child's eyes dropped toward the floor.
He had called it discipline.
But had he listened?
Had he been patient?
Had he made room for confession without crushing the person confessing?
For the first time, he wasn't searching his memory for examples of other people's theological failures.
He was remembering his own.
And it hurt.
Because conviction often begins where our favorite explanations finally run out.
Not every criticism is accurate. Not every accusation should be accepted without examination.
But neither should every criticism be dismissed simply because it threatens our self-image.
Sometimes God uses an uncomfortable conversation to bring us back to something we have been avoiding.
The man had spent years learning how to interpret difficult passages.
Now he needed to let a clear passage interpret his behavior.
James 1:22 says:
“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” — WEB
There it was.
The danger.
Not ignorance.
Self-deception.
He could hear the Word.
Explain the Word.
Defend the Word.
And still deceive himself if he refused to obey it.
And perhaps the most painful realization was this:
He had sometimes demanded repentance from others while treating repentance in his own life as an unnecessary interruption.
But the Gospel was never meant to make us experts at identifying everybody else's sin while remaining comfortable with our own.
Jesus asked:
“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but don't consider the beam that is in your own eye?” — Matthew 7:3, WEB
Jesus did not command us to abandon discernment.
In the verses that follow, He teaches that the beam must first be removed so that we can see clearly to help our brother.
The order matters.
Humility before correction.
Self-examination before accusation.
Repentance before self-righteous superiority.
And here is where the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because you may not be a Bible teacher.
You may not know Greek.
You may never have entered a formal theological debate.
But perhaps you know what it feels like to be right about someone's mistake and wrong about how you treated them.
Perhaps you have used silence to punish someone.
Perhaps you have withheld an apology because you believed the other person sinned first.
Perhaps you have shared powerful sermons about forgiveness while keeping a private list of people you refuse to forgive.
Perhaps you have defended Christian values publicly while neglecting Christian kindness privately.
Perhaps the people who know your theology best are the people who experience your patience least.
And perhaps, even now, part of you wants to think of someone else who needs to read this.
I understand.
It's easier to recognize pride when it belongs to another person.
But what if the Holy Spirit is inviting us to stop looking across the room and start looking into our own hearts?
Not to condemn us without hope.
But to lead us into repentance.
Because the most beautiful part of this story is not that the man was exposed.
It is that exposure did not have to be the end of his story.
He could have doubled down.
He could have defended himself.
He could have called the conversation an attack on biblical truth.
He could have walked away, convinced that nobody appreciated his faithfulness.
Instead, after a long silence, he whispered something he hadn't said sincerely in far too long.
“I think I've been proud.”
No speech.
No qualifications.
No carefully constructed defense.
Just the beginning of confession.
And then:
“I've hurt people while telling myself I was helping them.”
The words were difficult.
But for the first time that evening, he wasn't trying to win.
He was beginning to surrender.
That did not erase the damage.
It did not automatically restore every relationship.
It did not mean the people he had wounded were required to trust him immediately.
Repentance would need to become visible through changed behavior, patient listening, honest apologies, and consistent love.
But something had begun.
Not the abandonment of truth.
The abandonment of pride.
And that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to make arrogant sinners feel embarrassed about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
Including religious sinners.
Including self-righteous sinners.
Including people who have used the right words with the wrong hearts.
Including people who have confused spiritual authority with personal superiority.
Including you.
Including me.
The apostle Paul knew what it meant to be religiously zealous and profoundly wrong.
Before his conversion, he persecuted the church.
He later described himself as having been a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man, yet one who received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13).
The same man who once persecuted followers of Christ became a servant of the Christ he had opposed.
Not because his former actions were harmless.
Not because sincerity made persecution acceptable.
But because the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than the sins of those who truly turn to Him.
Paul wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, WEB
That is the Gospel.
Not that your theological knowledge can save you.
Not that your religious reputation can cleanse you.
Not that enough correct arguments can compensate for an unrepentant heart.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
At the cross, our pride finds no reason to boast.
Our sin is exposed.
God's justice is not ignored.
And His mercy is revealed through the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our accomplishments (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that same grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live differently (Titus 2:11–12).
Grace does not tell the proud person that pride is harmless.
Grace calls the proud person to come to Christ.
Grace does not excuse cruelty because the theology was technically correct.
Grace teaches us to repent and walk in love.
Grace does not require us to pretend that broken relationships have instantly healed.
Grace gives us the courage to confess, seek reconciliation where possible, and persevere in changed behavior.
And if you have spent years becoming someone who always has an answer but rarely offers an apology, hear this carefully.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life being the person your pride has made you.
In Christ, there is forgiveness.
In Christ, there is hope.
In Christ, there is a new way to live.
Ezekiel 36:26 contains God's promise to His people:
“I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” — WEB
The Hebrew phrase for “a new heart” is:
לֵב חָדָשׁ — lev chadash
A new heart.
In its original context, this promise concerns God's restoration and renewal of His people. It is not a guarantee that every stubborn personality will change overnight.
But it reveals something essential about God's saving work.
God is concerned with more than outward religious performance.
He transforms people from within.
And through the new covenant established by Jesus Christ, believers are called to live by the Spirit rather than merely maintain the appearance of righteousness.
That is why the fruit of the Spirit includes love, patience, kindness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).
Not merely impressive knowledge.
Not merely public confidence.
Not merely the ability to recognize someone else's error.
The Spirit produces a transformed life.
A life that increasingly reflects the character of Christ.
So imagine the man returning home after that conversation.
Imagine him standing outside his child's bedroom.
For once, he isn't rehearsing a lecture.
He isn't preparing a defense.
He knocks.
His child looks up.
And he says:
“I owe you an apology.”
The child waits.
“I've been harsh with you. I've interrupted you when you were trying to explain. I've acted like being your father means I never have to admit when I'm wrong.”
A pause.
“I was wrong. Will you forgive me?”
Perhaps the child cries.
Perhaps the child says nothing.
Perhaps trust takes time to rebuild.
But the father has finally begun to practice something he once knew only how to explain.
Humility.
Now imagine him speaking to his wife.
Listening without immediately correcting her description of the problem.
Acknowledging specific failures without adding the word “but.”
Accepting that an apology is not a transaction that purchases instant reconciliation.
Then imagine him opening his Bible the next morning.
The same Bible.
The same sacred words.
But a different posture.
Not hunting for ammunition.
Not searching for another argument to win.
Simply praying:
“Lord Jesus, teach me to obey what I know.”
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have been avoiding.
Not “Lord, show me who is wrong.”
But “Lord, show me where I need to repent.”
Not “Lord, make everyone recognize the truth I speak.”
But “Lord, make my life consistent with the truth I confess.”
Not “Lord, help me win this argument.”
But “Lord, help me love this person without compromising Your Word.”
Because Christianity is not a competition to see who can sound the most biblical.
It is a life of following Jesus Christ.
And following Jesus includes taking up our cross, denying ourselves, and learning from the One who is gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29; Luke 9:23).
That humility does not make truth negotiable.
It makes us more faithful in how we handle it.
We still correct error.
We still defend the Gospel.
We still reject teaching that contradicts Scripture.
But we do so remembering that we are servants, not saviors.
We point people to Christ.
We do not replace Christ with our own importance.
And if this story has exposed something in you, please don't bury it under another explanation.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Apologize where you have caused harm.
Seek help and accountability where patterns have become deeply rooted.
Open your Bible not merely to gather more information, but to hear and obey the Lord.
And remember that repentance is not the enemy of sound doctrine.
It is one of the proper responses to sound doctrine.
The deepest proof that you have understood the Gospel is not that you have become impossible to correct, but that you are learning to submit to the Christ who corrects you.
Maybe this article has brought someone to mind.
A pastor.
A teacher.
A parent.
A friend.
A spouse.
Someone who knows the Bible but struggles to show its love.
Before you send it to them, ask yourself one more question.
“What is Jesus asking me to change?”
Not to publicly shame a person.
Not to start another theological fight.

But because somewhere in your circle is a believer who has confused being right with being righteous, and somewhere else is a wounded soul who needs to know that the harshness they experienced does not represent the fullness of Christ's character.
And please, don't leave this as another article you read, agree with, and forget.
Return to it the next time you feel the urge to correct someone before listening.
Return to it before you respond to a disagreement online.
Return to it when an apology feels like defeat.
Because sometimes the Scripture we most need is not the one that helps us answer another person.
It is the one that brings us to repentance.
And I want to invite you into a conversation that matters more than another argument.
Maybe your word is humble.
Maybe it's patient.
Maybe it's gentle.
Maybe it's forgiving.
Maybe it's teachable.
Or perhaps all you can write today is:
You don't have to share private details or expose someone else's failures. Even a few sincere words can encourage another believer who is struggling with the same battle.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ has corrected your pride, restored your relationships, or taught you to speak the truth in love, consider sharing it.
Someone reading may need to know that change is possible.
That grace is real.
That repentance is not the end of the story.
At Gospel Warrior, this is why we keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, and pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
We don't want to build a community that simply knows more religious vocabulary.
We want to help cultivate believers who love God's Word, understand the Gospel, practice repentance, grow in discernment, and increasingly reflect the character of Christ.
Think of it as an opportunity to give regularly toward a ministry you believe is serving others through the Gospel.
Paul reminds us:
“Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, WEB
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not a promise that money purchases God's favor.
But joyful participation in work that seeks to make Jesus Christ known.
Because the mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
It is to make Jesus Christ known.
And now, before you leave, return to the man at the beginning of this story.
The man who could correct everyone else's theology.
The man who knew the Greek and Hebrew.
The man who had an answer for almost everything.
Until someone asked him about his character.
Perhaps you expected his story to end in humiliation.
But the Gospel offers something better than humiliation.
It offers repentance and grace.
He didn't need to throw away his theological books.
He needed to lay down his pride.
He didn't need to stop loving biblical truth.
He needed to stop using biblical truth as a shield against personal correction.
He didn't need less Jesus.
He needed to surrender more fully to the Jesus he had spent so many years explaining.
And perhaps, tonight, that is where your own story begins to change.
Not when you win your next argument.
Not when someone finally admits that you were right.
Not when your biblical knowledge impresses another person.
But when you kneel before the Lord and whisper:

“Jesus, I've been so busy examining everyone else's walk with You that I've neglected my own. Forgive me. Teach me to love Your truth enough to obey it. Teach me to correct with gentleness, listen with humility, and repent without excuses. Make me more like You.”
That prayer doesn't earn salvation.
Christ alone saves.
But it may be the beginning of a beautiful return to obedience for someone who has spent too long confusing knowledge with maturity.
Because the final question is not merely whether you can explain the character of Jesus.
It is whether, by His grace, you are becoming more like Him.
You may have won every argument in the room… but the moment you finally surrendered your pride to Jesus may be the moment grace began rewriting what your arguments never could.
